title: Consider It Pure Joy
subtitle: James 1:1–12
description: The letter opens hard: trials counted as pure joy, wisdom asked in faith without doubting, the rich fading like a flower, and a crown for the man who perseveres.
paragraphs: Some letters in this series run long and wind through travel plans, old arguments, and news from a dozen towns. This one is short, blunt, and built like a string of short lessons from a teacher who expects to be obeyed. It signs itself in a single line and tells us almost nothing else about its writer: “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.” No life story follows, and none will be supplied here. His whole greeting is one word at the end of the address: “To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion: Greetings.” The series places this letter among the undated books, because the text gives no date for itself. What it gives instead, starting in its second sentence, is instruction, and the first instruction is one of the hardest in the whole letter.

James does not ease his hearers toward it. “Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you encounter trials of many kinds,” he says, and he gives his reason in the same breath: “because you know that the testing of your faith develops perseverance.” The trials are not called pleasant, and they are not called good in themselves. They are called a testing, and a testing has a result. What it builds, if it is allowed to build anything, is perseverance, and perseverance has its own assignment: “Allow perseverance to finish its work, so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything.” Mature and complete, lacking nothing. That is where James says the road through trouble runs, and he says it before he says anything about how to get out of the trouble.

Trouble raises questions nobody can answer alone, and James knows it. “Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God,” he says, and he describes the God who is asked as one “who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him.” Generously, to all, without finding fault: the asker will not be scolded for needing to ask. But there is a condition, and it cuts. “But he must ask in faith, without doubting, because he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.” A wave goes wherever the wind pushes it, first one way, then the other, and James says a doubting asker should expect the same instability in his praying to follow him home: “That man should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.”

Then, without pausing, the teaching turns to money, and it turns the world upside down in two sentences. “The brother in humble circumstances should exult in his high position,” James says. The poor believer, low in every ranking his neighbors keep, is told to boast, because in God's ranking he stands high. The rich man gets the mirror image: “the one who is rich should exult in his low position, because he will pass away like a flower of the field.” His wealth is a flower, real and beautiful and already fading. James paints it in one hot picture: “For the sun rises with scorching heat and withers the plant; its flower falls and its beauty is lost. So too, the rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.” Not at the end of his pursuits. In the midst of them, busy and prospering, the fading is already at work.

The opening lesson ends where it began, with the man still standing inside the trial. “Blessed is the man who perseveres under trial,” James says, “because when he has stood the test, he will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him.” Blessed, standing, tested, crowned: the words stack up in that order, and the crown is not called a payment. It is a promise, made by God himself, and it is aimed at a particular kind of person, the one who loves him. James has only just begun, and his hearers have already been told what to do with trouble, how to ask for wisdom, and how little their money will matter. The lessons come this fast for the whole letter.

title: Every Good and Perfect Gift
subtitle: James 1:13–18
description: Temptation is traced to its own home in desire, and set against the opposite chain: every good and perfect gift coming down from an unchanging Father.
paragraphs: The first lesson ended with a crown for the man who stands the test. The second guards the test itself, because a person under pressure can start blaming the wrong source. “When tempted, no one should say,” James writes, and he puts the forbidden sentence out in the open: “God is tempting me.” That charge is not allowed, and the reason is stated flatly: “For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone.” Evil cannot get at God as a temptation, and God does not hand evil out as one. Whatever is pulling at a man inside his trial, it did not come from heaven.

So where does temptation come from? James traces it much closer to home: “But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed.” The pull starts with a man's own desires, and the desires do the luring. Then James follows the chain to its end in one sentence built like a family line: “Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.” Desire conceives. Sin is born. Sin, given time to grow up, produces death. Nothing in the chain is blamed on God, and nothing in it stands still. Left alone, it grows.

That is why the next line is a warning before it is a comfort: “Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers.” The deception James fears is a wrong picture of what God sends, so he corrects the picture at its top: “Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights.” Down is the direction of gifts. Temptation rises from a man's own desires; good and perfect gifts come down from the Father. The two streams do not share a source, and James will not let his brothers mix them.

The Father of the heavenly lights is not like the lights he made. Sun, moon, and stars move across the sky, and their shadows swing and shift with them, but of God James says he is the one “with whom there is no change or shifting shadow.” He does not brighten and darken. He does not give generously one day and tempt the next. The God who cannot be tempted by evil is the same God in every season, and the gifts that come down from him are good all the way down.

Then James names what this unchanging God has already given his hearers, and it answers the grim birth chain of verse 15 with a birth of a different kind: “He chose to give us birth through the word of truth, that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creation.” Desire gives birth to sin, and sin to death. God, by his own choice, gives birth through the word of truth, and what is born is called firstfruits, the first portion of a harvest that belongs to him. Six verses hold both births side by side, and the whole lesson rests on keeping them separate: death grows out of a man's own desires, and life is a gift that comes down from a Father who does not change.

title: Doers of the Word
subtitle: James 1:19–27
description: Quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger; the word received with humility; the man in the mirror; and religion tested at the tongue and at the widow's door.
paragraphs: The teaching turns from what God gives to how his people receive it, and it starts with three speeds: “My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” Quick, slow, slow. Listening is to be fast and anger is to be last, and James gives the reason without softening it: “for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.” A man can feel his anger rising like proof that he cares about what is right, and James says it produces none of what God wants. The righteous life God desires does not grow out of human anger.

So the ground has to be cleared and something better planted in its place: “Therefore, get rid of all moral filth and every expression of evil, and humbly accept the word planted in you, which can save your souls.” Getting rid and accepting stand back to back. Filth and evil are taken off like dirty clothes, and the word is received with humility, as something planted that a man did not grow himself. This word, James says, is not information. It can save souls, which is why what a hearer does with it matters so much in everything that follows.

That doing is the blunt center of the chapter: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Otherwise, you are deceiving yourselves.” Hearing without doing is not a halfway obedience in James's accounting; it is a self deception. He explains it with the most ordinary object in a house: “For anyone who hears the word but does not carry it out is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror,” a man who studies his own face, “and after observing himself goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like.” The mirror told him the truth. It showed him exactly what he looked like. Walking away and forgetting wastes the whole look, and James says hearing the word and not carrying it out wastes the hearing the same way.

The man in the mirror is not the only man in the illustration. Against him James sets the one who stays and looks: “But the one who looks intently into the perfect law of freedom, and continues to do so.” This looker is marked by two things: he is “not being a forgetful hearer, but an effective doer,” and his reward is not postponed to some distant day: “he will be blessed in what he does.” Blessed in the doing itself. The law he looks into is called a law of freedom, and the freedom shows itself in a hearer who keeps looking and then acts on what he saw.

The chapter closes by testing religion at two points where it cannot hide. The first is the mouth: “If anyone considers himself religious and yet does not bridle his tongue, he deceives his heart and his religion is worthless.” A man can rate his own religion highly, and one unbridled tongue cancels the rating. The second test is what true religion does with its hands: “Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world.” Orphans and widows, the people with the least protection in their world, are named as the care that counts before God, and the man who cares for them is to stay unpolluted by the very world that neglected them. That is chapter 1's last word: religion God calls pure is measured at the tongue, at the door of the widow, and nowhere less.

title: Do Not Show Favoritism
subtitle: James 2:1–13
description: A supposed meeting, two seats, and the royal law: favoritism named as sin and lawbreaking, and mercy set to triumph over judgment.
paragraphs: Chapter 2 opens with a flat rule that sits on top of everything the letter has said so far: “My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism.” Faith in a glorious Lord and favoritism toward people do not belong together, and James does not argue the point in the abstract. He builds a scene and tells his hearers to suppose it is happening in their own meeting, which means it stays his supposition, a picture held up for inspection, not a report of something that occurred.

Here is the picture. “Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in shabby clothes also comes in.” Two men, one door, and the difference between them is entirely in what they wear. Then the ushers in the picture do what James is afraid his hearers do: “If you lavish attention on the man in fine clothes and say,” and the welcome pours out, “Here is a seat of honor,” “but say to the poor man,” and the poor man gets the leftovers, “You must stand” or “Sit at my feet.” The rich man is seated by his clothes. The poor man is placed by his, on the floor at someone's feet, and both placements happen inside a meeting of people who claim faith in Jesus Christ.

James asks the question the picture was built to force: “have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?” Judges, he calls them, and corrupt ones. Then he turns the rankings over. “Listen, my beloved brothers: Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him?” The man pushed to the floor is, in God's choosing, rich in faith and an heir. “But you have dishonored the poor. Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court?” The very class of people honored in the meeting is the class hauling the believers into court. “Are they not the ones who blaspheme the noble name by which you have been called?” Honor is flowing toward the blasphemers and away from the heirs, and James calls that what it is.

His ground is the law itself. “If you really fulfill the royal law stated in Scripture,” the law that says, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” then, he grants, “you are doing well.” That command is quoted from Leviticus, and James calls it royal. But the same law that honors the neighbor condemns the sorting of neighbors: “But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.” And there is no partial credit for keeping the rest of it: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it.” James proves the unity of the law from its one Speaker: “For He who said,” “Do not commit adultery,” “also said,” “Do not murder.” One voice stands behind both commands, so a man who keeps one and breaks the other has not obeyed a list; he has defied a Lawgiver: “If you do not commit adultery, but do commit murder, you have become a lawbreaker.”

The section ends by aiming the whole thing at the judgment to come: “Speak and act as those who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom.” Speech and action, both, are to be carried on by people who know they will be judged, and by a law of freedom at that. And over that judgment James sets one sentence of hope that has carried believers ever since: “For judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment.” The merciless face a merciless standard. But mercy, the very thing favoritism refuses the poor man, is stronger than the judgment seat it stands before.

title: Faith Without Deeds Is Dead
subtitle: James 2:14–26
description: Faith without deeds put on trial in James's own order: the empty blessing, the demons who shudder, Abraham on the mountain, Rahab at the door, and a body without breath.
paragraphs: James now takes up the claim his whole letter has been circling, and he asks about it in the form of a profit question: “What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him?” A claim is the thing under examination, not a man James names, and his test case is as plain as the favoritism scene before it: “Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food.” Need, standing in the room, with nothing on and nothing to eat. “If one of you tells him,” says James, and out comes the warm dismissal, “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,” “but does not provide for his physical needs, what good is that?” The words wished the need away and met none of it. Then the verdict lands on faith itself: “So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.”

James stages the argument the way a teacher stages an objector, giving the other side its line so he can answer it in the open: “But someone will say,” and the line goes, “You have faith and I have deeds.” Two separate packages, faith for one man and deeds for another, as if the two could be divided between them. James refuses the division: “Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds.” Faith that cannot be shown is challenged to produce itself, and his own faith, he says, is visible in what it does. Then he presses the objector's faith down to its bare content: “You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that,” he says, and shudder at it. Belief that God is one is true belief, and demons hold it, and all it earns them is terror. Belief by itself, even correct belief, is not the living thing James is after.

Then he asks for permission to present his evidence: “O foolish man, do you want evidence that faith without deeds is worthless?” The first witness is the father of the nation: “Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?” James reads Abraham's offering as faith at work, not faith replaced: “You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did.” And the old Scripture about Abraham is not set aside by this; James says it was completed by it: “And the Scripture was fulfilled that says,” and here he quotes Genesis, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” “and he was called a friend of God.” Believed God, credited as righteousness, called a friend of God: James holds the believing and the offering together in one man and will not pull them apart.

From Abraham he draws his conclusion in the open: “As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone.” And his second witness is deliberately chosen from the opposite end of Israel's story: “In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route?” Even Rahab, James says. The Canaanite woman who hid Israel's spies in Jericho is set beside Abraham the father of Israel, and the same word is spoken over both of them, because in both of them faith acted. James gives both stories exactly this much room and no more; their full tellings stand in their own books, and here they serve as his witnesses, called and heard in two verses each.

The section ends with a body lying still: “As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.” A body with no spirit in it is not a resting body or an incomplete one; it is a corpse. That is James's final picture of the claim he started with, faith professed and never acted on. The chapter that began with a poor man sent to sit on the floor ends with the reason the whole thing matters: the faith that receives him, feeds him, and clothes him is alive, and the faith that only talks is not faith in any sense James will recognize. It is a body with nothing in it.

title: No Man Can Tame the Tongue
subtitle: James 3:1–12
description: Teachers warned first, then the tongue in three pictures: bit and rudder, spark and forest, spring and fig tree, blessing and cursing out of the same mouth.
paragraphs: Chapter 3 begins with a warning aimed at the people most tempted to use words for a living: “Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly.” We, James says, putting himself under the same stricter judgment as every other teacher. Teaching multiplies words, and words are the one field where nobody's record is clean: “We all stumble in many ways. If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to control his whole body.” The tongue is presented as the hardest member to govern, the one whose mastery would mean mastery of everything else. What follows is James explaining why, and he explains it with three pictures of small things steering large ones.

The first two pictures are about control. “When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can guide the whole animal.” A small piece of metal in a horse's mouth turns the whole horse. “Consider ships as well. Although they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined.” A ship big enough to fight strong winds answers to a small rudder set where the pilot pleases. Bit and rudder agree: small instruments, enormous reach. James draws the line to the mouth: “In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things.” Small, like the bit. Small, like the rudder. And able, like both of them, to direct the whole.

The third picture is not about control but about loss of it: “Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze.” Then James drops the comparisons and says the thing itself, at full strength: “The tongue also is a fire, a world of wickedness among the parts of the body. It pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.” A world of wickedness, carried in one small member. It pollutes the whole person, the whole course of a life set burning by words, and behind the tongue's fire James names a darker one feeding it. Nothing in the letter so far has been said this strongly, and James does not step back from it.

Man, who tames everything else, cannot tame this. “All kinds of animals, birds, reptiles, and creatures of the sea are being tamed and have been tamed by man,” James writes, running through the whole created order, land, air, and sea, “but no man can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.” Restless: it will not stay still or stay quiet. Poison: what it carries can kill. Every wild creature in the world has met its tamer, and the one creature no man has ever brought under control is the one inside his own mouth.

The proof James offers is the double work every hearer recognizes in himself: “With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness.” One tongue, two directions, blessing aimed up at God and cursing aimed across at men made in God's own likeness. “Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this should not be!” Then he asks nature to judge it: “Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring?” “My brothers, can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs? Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water.” Springs give one kind of water. Trees bear their own kind of fruit. The mouth that blesses and curses is doing what no spring and no tree in God's world can do, and James leaves it there, an impossibility his hearers perform every day.

title: Wisdom from Above
subtitle: James 3:13–18
description: Two wisdoms named and marked: the counterfeit that is earthly, unspiritual, demonic, and the wisdom from above, pure first, sown in peace by peacemakers.
paragraphs: After the tongue, James turns to the thing the tongue usually claims to be carrying: wisdom. His test for it is not talk. “Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom.” Show it, he says, the same demand he made of faith in the last chapter. Wisdom in James's school is demonstrated the way faith is, by deeds, and the deeds have a particular flavor: they are done in humility, the humility that real wisdom produces. A man who has to announce his wisdom has already failed the examination James is giving.

There is a counterfeit on the market, and James names its ingredients in the heart: “But if you harbor bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast in it or deny the truth.” Harbor is his word; jealousy and ambition are kept like guests in the house of the heart. A man can dress that mixture up as wisdom, boast in it, and call it insight, and James orders two things: do not boast in it, and do not deny the truth about what it is. Boasting about bitter jealousy is lying with a straight face, and the first step James commands is simply to stop calling the thing by a better name.

Then he gives the counterfeit its true name, all three words at full weight: “Such wisdom does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.” Earthly: it belongs to this world's way of climbing. Unspiritual: the Spirit has no part in it. Demonic: James reaches past human failure and names a darker origin, the same plainness with which he called the tongue set on fire by hell. And its fruit matches its root: “For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice.” Disorder, and not one evil practice but every kind. Where the harboring goes on, the community comes apart, and James says the connection is certain enough to state as a law.

Against that portrait he sets the real thing, described in the longest single sentence of the chapter: “But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere.” First of all pure: purity stands at the head of the list before peace is even mentioned. Then peace-loving, gentle, willing to yield ground, full of mercy and the good fruit mercy grows, impartial between the rich man and the poor man of chapter 2, and sincere, with nothing underneath the surface that differs from the surface. Every word in the list is a word about how a person treats other people. Wisdom from above is recognizable the way a tree is, by what grows on it.

The chapter closes in a field: “Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness.” Sowing and reaping are slow work, done in season, and James assigns the harvest to a specific kind of farmer: peacemakers, people who plant peace the way a man plants seed, in rows, on purpose, expecting a crop. What comes up is the fruit of righteousness, the very righteousness James said back in chapter 1 that man's anger cannot produce. Anger cannot grow it. Jealousy and ambition cannot grow it. It grows where peace is sown by people made wise from above, and chapter 3 ends with that quiet picture after all its fire.

title: Friendship with the World
subtitle: James 4:1–10
description: The battlefield moved inside, prayer bent by desire, the sharpest address in the letter, Proverbs' grace to the humble, and the string of commands that leads out.
paragraphs: Chapter 4 opens by moving the battlefield. The conflicts tearing at these believers look like fights between people, and James asks where they actually start: “What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from the passions at war within you?” The war is inside before it is between. Then he describes the inner war's casualties in blunt sequence: “You crave what you do not have; you kill and covet, but are unable to obtain it. You quarrel and fight. You do not have, because you do not ask.” Craving that cannot obtain turns outward into quarreling, and through the whole scramble runs one strange fact: these people are not asking God. The desires wage their war everywhere except in prayer.

Even the praying, when it happens, is bent by the same desires: “And when you do ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures.” God is treated as a supplier for the very passions that started the wars. Then James names the whole arrangement with the harshest address in the letter: “You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God? Therefore, whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God.” Adulteresses: the word pictures a marriage broken by a second love, God on one side and the world wooing on the other, and James says friendship with the second is hostility toward the first. No one drifts into being God's enemy in this sentence; he chooses the friendship, and the enmity follows.

James supports the charge with a Scripture line, and here the telling has to show a seam honestly. He writes, “Or do you think the Scripture says without reason” that “the Spirit He caused to dwell in us yearns with envy?” James attributes the line to Scripture, and it matches no single passage in the older Scriptures word for word. The telling quotes him as he writes it and assigns the line no address he did not give it. What follows the seam, though, is the turn of the whole chapter: “But He gives us more grace. This is why it says:” and here James quotes Proverbs directly, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” More grace: greater than the envy, greater than the warring passions, and it flows in one direction, toward the humble, while the proud meet opposition from God himself.

The way out is a string of commands, and they come in pairs. “Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” Down before God, standing against the devil, and the devil's flight is promised as the result. “Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.” Hands and hearts both, outward action and inward loyalty, and the double-minded of chapter 1 are back, still being called to be single. The road toward God in James is not a mood. It is submission, resistance, nearness, and washing, in that order.

The last commands go deeper than behavior, into feeling itself: “Grieve, mourn, and weep. Turn your laughter to mourning, and your joy to gloom.” The laughter James targets is the laughter of people at ease with their own warring and befriending, and he orders it exchanged for mourning, because mourning agrees with the truth about their state and laughter does not. Then the chapter's whole movement lands on the promise that answers Proverbs: “Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you.” Grace to the humble, exaltation to the humbled. James's hearers can fight their passions for what they crave and obtain nothing, or go low before the Lord and be lifted by the hand they submitted to. Chapter 4 leaves the choice standing open in those two postures.

title: You Are a Mist
subtitle: James 4:11–17
description: Slander and the occupied judge's seat, then the planners called out by their own words, life as a mist, and the sin of knowing the right thing and not doing it.
paragraphs: The chapter that began with wars inside the heart ends with two quieter sins, and the first is done with the mouth: “Brothers, do not slander one another. Anyone who speaks against his brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it.” James traces what a slandering man is actually doing, and it is bigger than an unkind remark. To set oneself over a brother is to set oneself over the law that commands love of that brother: “And if you judge the law, you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it.” Practitioner or judge: a man stands either under the law doing it, or above the law grading it, and the slanderer has quietly changed seats.

The seat he has taken is already occupied. “There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?” One Lawgiver, one Judge, and his credentials are stated in the two powers no human judge holds together, to save and to destroy. Against that, James's question is almost gentle, and it is unanswerable on its own terms. The neighbor is the very man the royal law of chapter 2 commands the hearer to love as himself. Judging him is not a small fault of temper for James; it is a man climbing into a chair that belongs to God.

Then James turns and calls out a second group by their own words: “Come now, you who say,” and he quotes the plan in their own confident grammar, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit.” City chosen, calendar set, business named, profit assumed. It is an ordinary business plan, the kind merchants made every week, and James's objection is not to planning. It is to the certainty. Not one word in the plan leaves room for anything the planners do not control, and their whole year rests on a tomorrow they have not been given.

His answer is the picture this episode is named for: “You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.” A mist: visible for a moment over the field, gone when the sun is on it. That, James says, is the length and solidity of the life doing all this scheduling. In place of the old grammar he gives them another sentence to say: “Instead, you ought to say,” and the replacement runs, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.” Four words at the front of the plan change its whole ownership. Life itself, not just profit, is held at the Lord's willing, and the plan is spoken as a hope instead of a possession.

James closes the chapter by calling the old way what it is and then widening the definition of sin past where most people stop: “As it is, you boast in your proud intentions. All such boasting is evil.” Proud intentions, boasted in, are evil even before a single plan succeeds or fails. And then the last verse, a sentence that reaches back over the whole letter: “Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin.” Sin is not only the wrong thing done. It is the right thing known and left undone, the deed chapter 2 demanded, the care chapter 1 called pure religion. James's hearers now know a great deal of right. By his final standard, knowing it has raised what is required of them.

title: Weep and Wail, You Rich
subtitle: James 5:1–6
description: The rich addressed in the open: rotted riches, corroded gold, wages crying out from the fields, and the righteous man who did not resist, in six verses.
paragraphs: Chapter 5 opens with the same call James used on the boasting merchants, “come now,” only this time there is no argument to answer, just a sentence to hear: “Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery to come upon you.” Weep and wail now, he says, over a misery still on its way. The rich men of chapter 2, the ones who oppress the believers and drag them into court, are addressed directly at last, and James speaks to them the way the old prophets spoke to doomed cities, in certainties, most of them already stated in the past tense, as if the ruin had happened.

He inventories their wealth, and every item in the inventory is damaged goods: “Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes.” Riches rotted like stored food left too long. Clothes, the very thing the rich man of chapter 2 wore into the meeting to win his seat of honor, eaten through by moths in the closet. What they stored up has been quietly spoiling in storage. The hoard did not wait for judgment day to begin testifying; it started decaying the day it was shut away, and James reads the decay as evidence.

Even the metals, the part of wealth that cannot rot, are entered as ruined: “Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire. You have hoarded treasure in the last days.” Gold does not rust in the ordinary way of things, and that is part of the force of it: in James's picture even the incorruptible wealth has a corrosion on it, and the corrosion has two jobs. It will testify, standing up in the judgment like a witness for the prosecution, and it will consume, burning the hoarders like the fire of chapter 3. And the charge itself is timed: the hoarding was done in the last days, treasure piled up by men who acted as if the days would never end.

Then James points at a sound: “Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.” The wages themselves cry out, money kept back from the men who cut the fields, and behind the unpaid money stand the unpaid men, crying too. Their cries have a destination and they have arrived: the ears of the Lord of Hosts, the Lord of heaven's armies. The rich men may never have answered the harvesters. Heaven has heard them, and heaven's hearing is the fact James leaves hanging over every luxury that follows.

The last two charges are the shortest and the heaviest. “You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter.” Fattened hearts: livestock language, animals fed richly for a killing day they do not see coming, applied to men feeding themselves. And then the final count: “You have condemned and murdered the righteous, who did not resist you.” The righteous man went down without resisting, condemned in the courts the rich controlled. James offers no closing appeal in this section, no way back stated, because the section is not an appeal; it is a verdict read aloud ahead of time. The brothers, when James turns back to them in the next verse, will be told to be patient under exactly this pressure, and they will know exactly who is standing on the other side of it.

title: The Prayer of a Righteous Man
subtitle: James 5:7–20
description: The letter closes whole: the farmer's patience, the prophets and Job, the rule about oaths, prayer and song and oil, Elijah's rain, and a wanderer turned back.
paragraphs: The verdict on the rich is read, and James turns back to the brothers living under their pressure with the letter's great closing word: patience. “Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord’s coming. See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil,” and, James adds, “how patient he is for the fall and spring rains.” A farmer cannot hurry a crop. He waits through two rainy seasons for fruit he calls precious, and the waiting is not idleness; it is the job. “You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord’s coming is near.” Strengthen your hearts, set them fast, and the reason is nearness. And while they wait, one habit is forbidden: “Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged. Look, the Judge is standing at the door!” The Judge of chapter 4, the one Lawgiver who saves and destroys, is pictured at the threshold, and people with a Judge at the door do not spend the wait prosecuting each other.

For examples of how to endure, James points backward, briefly, the way he pointed at Abraham and Rahab: “Brothers, as an example of patience in affliction, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.” Then one name is given its own sentence: “See how blessed we consider those who have persevered. You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.” Job's full story stands in its own book in this series, and James adds nothing to it here beyond the outcome and the character of the Lord who brought it: compassion and mercy are what the perseverance ran into at the end. Folded into the same passage is the rule about speech under pressure: “Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath.” Simply let your Yes be yes and your No be no, James says, “so that you will not fall under judgment.” Plain words, plainly meant, with no heaven or earth called in as collateral.

Then the letter's last movement gathers up the community's whole life into prayer, state by state. “Is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises.” Suffering prays and cheerfulness sings, and neither state is left without its response. For sickness the response is shared: “Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.” And the promise attached is carried exactly as James writes it: “And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.” The raising is the Lord's, the forgiveness is the Lord's, and James simply sets the promise down at full strength, the way he has set down every hard and hopeful thing in this letter.

From the elders' prayer James widens the practice to everyone: “Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.” Confession runs sideways, to each other, and prayer runs sideways too, and healing is found along that road. His proof is one man: “Elijah was a man just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years.” Just like us: that is the point of choosing him. “Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops.” Elijah's own full story stands earlier in this series; here he is compressed into two prayers and two weathers, evidence that the prayer of an ordinary, righteous man reaches the sky.

The letter has no farewell. Its last words are about rescue: “My brothers, if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back,” James says, consider what that bringing back is worth: “Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins.” A wanderer, a brother who goes after him, a soul saved from death, sins covered over in a multitude. After favoritism and dead faith, after the tongue's fire and the world's friendship, after hoarded gold and withheld wages, the teacher's final lesson is a brother turning a brother around. The letter ends on that errand, with no goodbye after it.
